unitTitles.4: Statistical inference: bivariate data and other procedures

toolsSub: The things you will reach for in every unit.

thinking.title: Statistical thinking: the big ideas
thinking.lead: Statistics is a way of thinking about the world wherever data, variation, and chance appear. It is more than a math requirement. It helps you question claims, not only calculate answers.

habits.title: Question the claim
habits.text: Who collected the data, how, and who is missing? Spotting bias is the first statistical skill.

habits.title: Expect variation
habits.text: No two samples are alike. Statistics asks what chance alone would produce before it asks what is surprising.

habits.title: Decide with evidence
habits.text: Probability and evidence let us make informed decisions without pretending to be certain.

thinking.doTitle: Two things you will be able to do well
do: Read a graph of data and say what it shows, and what it does not.
Take a statistical claim, run the right procedure, and write a conclusion that answers the claim.
thinking.closing: Data also shapes equity, culture, identity, and opportunity. Behind every dataset are people, and good statistical thinking keeps them in view.

ai.title: AI study partner
ai.sub: AI can support your learning when you use it thoughtfully. Try the problem yourself first, then use AI to get unstuck, check your thinking, and practice.
steps: Try the problem first. Write down what you tried and where you got stuck.
Pick a prompt that matches your problem. A Concept prompt is for when you do not understand the idea. A Skill prompt is for when you cannot get started or finish a problem.
Copy the prompt and paste it into Gemini, Claude, or ChatGPT. Replace every highlighted [bracket] with your problem, your work, or your numbers.
Answer the questions it asks you. A good study partner asks questions and gives hints. If it just gives you the answer, type: "Do not solve it for me. Ask me one question at a time."
Check what you learned. Compare the explanation with your guided notes or micro-lecture, then use a follow-up prompt to test yourself.
On an assignment, add one line saying how you used AI. Quizzes and exams are AI-free.
ai.followSub: Do not stop after the AI's first response. Use these follow-ups to push your learning deeper.
afterQuestions: What did I learn from this practice session? Did AI help me understand, or just give me an answer?
How does this explanation compare to what we learned in class or in the textbook?
What did I learn by questioning the AI's reasoning? How can I apply that thinking on an exam?
ai.waysTitle: Four ways to use AI to learn statistics
ai.waysSub: These work for any topic. Copy a prompt, fill in the brackets, and paste it into Gemini, Claude, or ChatGPT.

ways.title: AI as a brainstormer
ways.goal: Generate ideas, simplify a concept, or plan how to study.
prompts: I don't understand [concept]. Can you explain it simply?
What are 3 ways to think about [topic]?
How can I break down [topic] for my study guide?
ways.reflect: What ideas did AI suggest that you had not thought of? Which ones will you try, and why?

ways.title: AI as a searcher
ways.goal: Find explanations, definitions, or examples. Always verify what it tells you.
prompts: Summarize the idea of [topic] using examples and analogies.
What's the difference between a boxplot and a histogram?
Explain [topic] to me at three levels, from elementary school to college.
Can you give me 2 one-sample hypothesis test problems and walk me through them?
ways.reflect: How does this explanation compare to what we learned in class or in the textbook?

ways.title: AI as a tutor
ways.goal: Practice solving problems and get guidance. Always try first before asking for help.
prompts: Here's my solution to [problem]. Can you check my steps?
Give me a [type of] problem and help me if I get stuck.
I have an upcoming exam covering [topics]. Create a practice quiz for me and ask me each question one by one.
Turn [topic] into flashcard-style questions and answers.
ways.reflect: What did I learn from this practice session? Did AI help me understand, or just give me an answer?

ways.title: AI as a critical thinking partner
ways.goal: Question the AI's answers, ask "why" at every step, and compare approaches.
prompts: Why did you use a t-test instead of a z-test?
Is there another way to solve this problem?
Explain this visually instead of in words.
Compare my solution to yours and explain any differences.
ways.reflect: What did I learn by questioning the AI's reasoning? How can I apply that thinking during exams?

reminders: Try first, then check with AI. You learn more by attempting problems yourself.
Cross-reference AI responses with your notes, the textbook, or your instructor's materials.
Use AI ethically. Do not submit AI-written work as your own. Use it to learn, not to shortcut.

Here is a problem and my work: [paste problem and your steps]. Do not solve it for me. Find the first step where my reasoning goes wrong, explain why, and let me fix it myself.

S12.title: The mistake to watch for
S12.text: When the question is about a sample mean, divide σ by √n. "What is the probability of a result higher than 55?" is about one value. "A sample of 5 scores is collected. What is the probability the mean is higher than 55?" is about a sample mean, so it needs σ/√n.

items.label: Ask your class in Pronto
items.text: Post a picture of the problem. Explain what you do not understand or where you get stuck, and show what you already tried. Saying only "I am stuck" is not enough for us to help, so be as specific as you can. Pronto is for figuring out the thing you are missing, not for reteaching a whole concept.
